title: Head 2 · Setup & storage decisions
subtitle: Where vectors live, how the tables are shaped, and the ground rules that keep the laptop and the phone in step.
meta: Built; re-tested on two phones (3 Nov), swept 1k–300k (EYKO-90) and fully tested with real vectors, a faster loop, all three tables and any extension (EYKO-100, 4 Nov). Open questions and their cards are in section 2.
Vector storage (sqlite-vec vs float32 BLOBs), the video memory tables, raw SQL without an ORM, laptop–phone parity, tests, tooling and licences.
EYKO-1 (video memory tables + BLOB vector tables), EYKO-31 (vector storage spike), EYKO-30 (pytest).

sections.title: Summary
blocks: Every later stage writes to and reads from the same SQLite database, so its shape had to be decided first. The open question was where the **vectors** (512 numbers per frame, 384 per caption) live. The first plan used **sqlite-vec**, a SQLite extension built for vector search. Before building on it, a short spike (EYKO-31) tested whether it works on Android at all.

It does not load on Android's platform SQLite. The fallback, plain **float32 BLOB columns loaded into memory once and searched by dot product**, met the limit set before the test (under 200 ms at 20,000 vectors on the slow phone: 81 ms). That became the design on both laptop and phone.

blocks.note: **Rule fixed before the test:** if sqlite-vec fails to load on a phone, use BLOBs, provided a query takes under 200 ms at 20,000 vectors on the slow phone. Fixing the pass mark first means the result cannot be argued into a decision afterwards.

blocks.note: **How to update:** when a card closes, change that question's Status, rewrite its Answer with the new numbers, add the result file to Evidence, and set Last updated. Never delete an old finding: if a new run disagrees, say so in the Answer.

blocks.h3: A1 · Did you actually run sqlite-vec on the phone, or read about it? Show me the error.

rows: We ran it, three times on two real phones: Samsung A32 on 12 Oct and again on 3 Nov, Pixel 9 Pro XL on 3 Nov. Every run gives the same two errors: "no such module: vec0" and "no such function: load_extension".

Install the app and test app from the phone kit (adb install -r), then: adb shell am instrument -w -e class com.eykon.memory.spike.VectorStorageSpikeTest com.eykon.memory.test/androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner. Save the log unedited with adb logcat -d -s EYKO31.

docs/results/vectors/proof/a32-2026-11-03-logcat.txt, pixel9proxl-2026-11-03-logcat.txt and their -device.txt sheets; first run: docs/results/2026-10-12-eyko-31-vector-storage.md (Raw phone output); test code: android/app/src/androidTest/.../spike/VectorStorageSpikeTest.kt; commit 79f3904.
Add a screen recording and the Infinix run (EYKO-94).

blocks.h3: A2 · Is that a sqlite-vec problem or an Android problem?

rows: An Android problem. On both phones (Android 13 / SQLite 3.32.2 and Android 17 / SQLite 3.50.6) load_extension itself does not exist: it fails the same way for sqlite-vec and for a made-up extension name. Only modules compiled into the platform SQLite work, and of fts4, fts5 and rtree only fts4 does. So no loadable extension can run on the platform SQLite of either phone.
EYKO-100 extension check on the A32 and the Pixel, 4 Nov (section 6, "Full test").
Android's official reason (EYKO-89); a bundled SQLite is the only route left for sqlite-vec (EYKO-93).

blocks.h3: A3 · Android apps can ship their own SQLite. Did you try that route?

rows: Not yet. Only the built-in SQLite was tried. This is the main open point of the storage decision.
Planned: add a bundled SQLite (androidx sqlite-bundled or requery sqlite-android) with an arm64 sqlite-vec build on a throwaway branch, then time it against BLOBs.
EYKO-89 (which route), EYKO-93 (try it on the Pixel and A32).

blocks.h3: A4 · Did it fail only on one phone?

rows: Two phones so far: Samsung A32 (low-end, Helio G80) and Pixel 9 Pro XL (high-end, Tensor G4). Same failure on both.
Proof logs and device sheets for both phones.

blocks.h3: A5 · Do sqlite-vec and your BLOB search return the same results, or is one just faster?

rows: Both are exact search by design (no approximation), so they should return the same top 20. This has not been checked yet.
Planned: compare the top 20 of every method with exact numpy search (recall@20).

blocks.h3: B1 · One run? What is the spread?

rows: Each size now runs 20 queries × 5 runs after a warm-up. The 5 run medians stay within about 10 % on both phones (e.g. A32 20k: 77.2–84.5 ms; Pixel 20k: 40.1–41.1 ms). The 20k figure also matches the older single runs (81.0 ms on 12 Oct, 83.5 ms on 3 Nov). These were trial runs while charging; the protocol runs (EYKO-95) will add the Infinix and hot / low-battery conditions.
EYKO-90 sweep test on the A32 and the Pixel, 3 Nov (section 6, "Size sweep").

blocks.h3: B2 · Why only up to 20,000 vectors? When does a real user reach that?

rows: Measured up to 300k now. In-memory search passes 200 ms between 20k and 50k vectors on the A32 and between 50k and 100k on the Pixel; at 300k it runs out of memory on both. When a real user gets there is still an estimate: at about 13.4 kept frames per minute and an assumed one hour of video a day (~800 vectors a day), 20k comes in about 25 days, 50k in about 2 months and 100k in about 4 months. The hour a day is an assumption with no source yet.
EYKO-90 sweep (section 6); kept-frame rate from the Ego4D phone run (Head 8).
Real usage sources and the 1/3/6/12-month table (EYKO-101); Infinix (EYKO-95).

blocks.h3: B3 · Random vectors are not real ones. Does it hold with real data?

rows: For speed, yes. With real vectors from our own clips the times match the random ones (20k: A32 82 ms vs 80 ms random; Pixel 37 ms vs 40 ms). That is expected: an exact dot product does the same work whatever the numbers are. Whether search returns the right frames with real data is a retrieval question (Heads 7 and 8), not a storage one.
EYKO-100 sweep with -e source real on both phones (90 real vectors per table, padded with small noise).

blocks.h3: B4 · 112 MB of memory for one table: what about all three tables, on a 4 GB phone?

rows: Measured with all three tables loaded together (image 512, text 384, audio-sized 512; same rows each, the worst case). 20k rows each: app PSS 53 → 160 MB (A32) and 57 → 164 MB (Pixel), fits. 50k: out of memory while loading the third table on both phones; 100k: only the first table fits. The limit is the 268 MB Java heap Android gives the app, the same on the 6 GB A32 and the 16 GB Pixel. A 4 GB phone is not measured yet.
EYKO-100 memory test (Debug.getMemoryInfo after a garbage collection, before and after loading).
Infinix (EYKO-95, kit section 5c); the design answer in EYKO-98.

blocks.h3: B5 · The phone is about 50x slower than the laptop. Is that the chip or your code?

rows: Mostly our code. A faster loop (four running sums, keep the best 20 instead of sorting every row) returns the same top 20 on all 400 checks and is 5.9× faster on the A32 at 100k (537 → 91 ms); on the Pixel the gain is similar. The laptop has not been run with the same faster loop, so the remaining phone-vs-laptop gap is not measured yet. **Update 4 Nov (EYKO-102):** the faster scoring is now in the app. In the app's whole search the vector part was only a fifth to a quarter of the time; the rest was our code around it (reading frames, objects, sorting twice). Fixing all of it made the whole search 4.3× faster on the A32 and 4.1× on the Pixel at 20k, same hits (Head 7).
EYKO-100: both loops on the same vectors and queries, same run.
Sweep-real CSVs (blob_memory_dot vs blob_memory_fast, note column); Figure 4.
Same loop on the laptop (EYKO-91); moving the loop into the app is a lead decision.

blocks.h3: B6 · Does a hot phone or a low battery slow it down?

rows: Not measured. The 3 Nov Pixel run was charging at 36 °C, so it is not a clean baseline.
Planned: cool, hot (10 min load) and low-battery runs under a fixed protocol.

blocks.h3: B7 · Brute force will not scale. What is the plan past the limit?

rows: Measured limits: with the faster loop, speed stays under 200 ms past 100k vectors on both phones, so speed is no longer the first limit. Memory is: with all three tables in memory the app runs out between 20k and 50k rows. The plan past that is open. Candidates: int8 or float16 vectors (a quarter or half the memory), keeping only the image table in memory, loading in blocks, an approximate index (usearch, hnswlib) or bundled sqlite-vec. **Update 4 Nov (EYKO-102):** the real search (Head 7) is over 200 ms on the A32 from about 20k kept frames even after the speed-up (302 ms), and the first search after opening takes 2.0 s. So both speed and memory limit the design before 50k.
EYKO-90 sweep and EYKO-100 (section 6). Options not tested yet.
EYKO-89 and EYKO-91 (options), EYKO-93 (bundled sqlite-vec), EYKO-101 (when a user gets there), EYKO-98 (decision).

blocks.h3: B8 · Why was reading from disk twice as slow on the Pixel as on the cheaper A32?

rows: Seen again in the sweep: reading 20k vectors from SQLite on every query took 3,137–3,489 ms on the Pixel vs 1,569–1,627 ms on the A32, while from memory the Pixel was twice as fast. Still not explained. The Pixel was charging, 98 % full and reached 38 °C. It does not affect the app, which searches from memory.
EYKO-90 sweep, same day, both phones.
Repeat after freeing Pixel storage (EYKO-83) and under the protocol (EYKO-95).

blocks.h3: C1 · Prove the phone and the laptop store the same thing.

rows: One table design (src/video_memory/schema.py) is copied into the phone (VideoSchema.kt). On 4 Ego4D clips the phone and laptop kept the same frames (354 of 372 at the same second) with 99 % same place and 96 % same action. There is no automatic test that the two schemas are identical.
Schema parity test on both sides (EYKO-98).

blocks.h3: C2 · What does an hour of video cost in storage?

rows: One measured point: the database grew about 7 MB for 27.8 minutes of video, with every vector. Frame pictures were 8.8 MB per minute before dropped frames were deleted (EYKO-59).
Database size before and after the Ego4D phone run.
At least 4 points on the Infinix (EYKO-96).

blocks.h3: C3 · What happens if the app is killed in the middle of writing?

rows: By design the job saves the stage it reached and resumes there, and the link check fails the job if anything is missing. This is covered by tests on the laptop and phone, but nobody has killed the app mid-stage on a real phone and checked.
JVM and on-device tests of the queue and the link check.
9 force-stops at 3 stages on the Infinix (EYKO-96).

blocks.h3: C4 · Why no ORM (Room entities)?

rows: So the same SQL runs on the laptop (sqlite3) and the phone (SupportSQLiteDatabase) and the two cannot drift. Written down in this document but not as an ADR, and there is no timing.
ADR with an insert / read timing (EYKO-98).

blocks.h3: C5 · You say the tests pass. How many, and what do they cover?

rows: 109 JVM tests and 104 on-device tests at the 2 Nov gap review. No coverage figure and no CI run log.
No card yet: coverage figure and a CI log.

blocks.h3: D1 · MobileCLIP is research-only and YOLOE is AGPL. Can this ever ship?

rows: Allowed while the project is academic. A licence list with a swap-out plan for each model has not been written.

blocks.h3: D2 · Can someone other than you reproduce the setup?

rows: The phone kit installs and runs from its README alone, with only adb, on two phones (A32 fresh install, Pixel update). Not yet done by another person or on another laptop.
Phone kit used step by step on both phones; three README fixes made from that use.
docs/phone-kit/README.md, kit folder D:\eykon-cache\phone-kit-2026-11-03 (SHA256SUMS.txt), proof device sheets; EYKO-99 comment.
Zara on her Infinix (EYKO-99), clean laptop clone (EYKO-92).

sections.title: Approach

blocks.h3: The vector storage spike (EYKO-31)

steps: Generate 5,000 and 20,000 random 512-dimension unit vectors (fixed seed) and 20 query vectors; ask for the top 20 each time.
Laptop: Python 3.10.6, SQLite 3.37.2, numpy 2.2.6, sqlite-vec 0.1.9 (task spike-laptop-vectors).
Phone: Samsung A32 (Helio G80, 6 GB RAM, Android 13), standing in for the Infinix Note 12, which was not available (task spike-android-vectors).
Try sqlite-vec on the phone through the same platform SQLite that Room 2.6.1 uses.
Time three ways of searching: BLOBs read from SQLite on every query, BLOBs loaded into memory once, and sqlite-vec.
Record file size, insert time and Java / native heap.

blocks.h3: The tables (EYKO-1)

blocks: One table design, written down once in src/video_memory/schema.py and copied into the phone's VideoSchema.kt. Each kept frame is tied to its video and its second, so every search result can show the exact moment.

blocks.h3: Ground rules set at the same time

bullets: **Raw SQL, no ORM:** the laptop uses sqlite3 directly; the phone runs plain SQL on SupportSQLiteDatabase. The same statements work on both.
**Parity:** same ONNX model files, same filter maths, same constants on laptop and phone. Golden frames must give the same result on both, checked by tests.
**Tests:** pytest as a dev dependency on the laptop (task test, task smoke); JVM unit tests and on-device tests on the phone.
**Tooling:** uv for Python packages, Taskfile for every repeatable command, models and datasets on D:\eykon-cache, never in git.
**Licences:** AGPL (YOLOE) allowed while the project is academic; MobileCLIP is research-only and never shipped inside the app package.

blocks.h3: Re-run on 3 November 2026 (phone kit, two phones)

blocks: Raw logs and device sheets: docs/results/vectors/proof/ (commit 79f3904).

bullets: Real use since then: on the Pixel, the frame-vector search takes about 0.1 s (first search about 1 s while vectors load); storing a frame vector takes under 1 ms (Head 6).
Ego4D on the Pixel: the database grew about 7 MB for 27.8 minutes of video, with every vector (Head 8).

blocks.h3: Size sweep, 1k to 300k vectors (EYKO-90, two phones)

blocks: **Why:** the decision rested on one run of 20 queries at 5k and 20k only, so the supervisor's questions B1 (one run, what spread?) and B2 (why only 20k?) had no data. **Approach:** the same in-memory BLOB search the app uses (float32, dot product, top 20), measured at six sizes with repeats, on the cheap phone and the fast phone. The slow method (read the table from SQLite on every query) is kept as a comparison up to 20k only, because past that one query takes seconds.

steps: The test inserts n random unit vectors (512 numbers, fixed seed) into a fresh SQLite table, at n = 1k, 5k, 20k, 50k, 100k, 300k.
Per size and method: 1 warm-up query thrown away, then 20 queries × 5 runs; each run gives median, p95 and worst.

The test writes one CSV row per run (shared laptop/phone format) with Java heap, PSS, battery temperature and level. A size that runs out of memory is written as a row with the exact error, not skipped.

Command (phone kit README section 5b): adb shell am instrument -w -e class com.eykon.memory.spike.VectorStorageSpikeTest#blobColumnWithBruteForceSearch -e sizes 1k,5k,20k,50k,100k,300k -e commit 7fc6af7 com.eykon.memory.test/androidx.test.runner.AndroidJUnitRunner

cols: Pixel 9 Pro XL: median of the 5 runs (range)

blocks.caption: Figure 1. Search from memory, median of 20 queries; the bar on each point is the range of the 5 runs (too small to see on most). The 200 ms line is still an assumption (source: EYKO-101). Data: docs/results/vectors/*-sweep.csv.
Figure 2. Keeping the vectors in memory vs reading the table from SQLite on every query (log scale). Reading every time is over 200 ms from 5k on both phones.

Figure 3. The single block the vectors need against the Java heap limit both phones report (268 MB, even on the Pixel's 16 GB). 100k (205 MB) ran; 300k (614 MB) failed on both: "Failed to allocate a 614400016 byte allocation … growth limit 268435456".

blocks.note: **Outcome (good and bad):** the runs are stable (5 run medians within about 10 %), and the old 20k number holds (A32 80 ms now, 81 ms on 12 Oct). But in-memory search passes 200 ms between **20k and 50k on the A32** and between **50k and 100k on the Pixel**, and above roughly 100k–130k vectors the table **cannot be held in memory at all** with the current design. The design is fine for small libraries and has a hard ceiling for large ones.

blocks: **Not yet protocol runs:** both phones were charging at low battery; the Infinix and the protocol runs (cool, hot, low battery) come from EYKO-95. **Next:** how many vectors a real user reaches (EYKO-101), real vectors and honest memory with all three tables (EYKO-100), and the storage decision v2 (EYKO-98). Graphs: uv run docs/documents/source/figures/vector_sweep.py redraws them from every sweep CSV.

blocks.h3: Full test: real vectors, a faster loop, all three tables, any extension (EYKO-100)

blocks: **Why:** the size sweep left four supervisor questions open: A2 (is it sqlite-vec or Android?), B3 (random vectors are not real ones), B4 (memory with all tables) and B5 (is the slowness the chip or our code?). **Approach:** one change per question, on the same two phones, same day.

steps: **Any extension (A2):** besides vec0, the test calls load_extension on a made-up name, tries the fts5, fts4 and rtree modules, and reads PRAGMA compile_options.

**Real vectors (B3):** 90 image and 90 text vectors from our own recordings (12–22 Oct, incl. the two kit clips; no Ego4D) are built into the test APK (src/benchmarks/export_own_vectors.py) and padded to each size with small noise. Queries are our frames with more noise.

**Faster loop (B5):** next to the app's loop (one running sum, then sort every row) the test runs a second loop: four running sums, and a 20-slot min-heap instead of a full sort. On every query it checks both give the same top 20.

**All three tables (B4):** image (512), text (384) and an audio-sized (512) table with the same number of rows each (the worst case) are loaded together the way the app loads them; total PSS (Debug.getMemoryInfo) after a garbage collection, before and after.
Commands: phone kit README sections 5b (-e source real) and 5c. The raw logs of both phones are in docs/results/vectors/proof/.

blocks.h3: The two search loops compared: what "app's loop" and "faster loop" mean

blocks: Every search does two jobs. **1. Score every stored vector:** multiply the query's 512 numbers with the stored vector's 512 numbers, pair by pair, and add them up (the dot product; our vectors have length 1, so this is the cosine similarity: higher means more alike). **2. Keep the best 20.** Both loops do exactly these two jobs on exactly the same numbers; they differ only in **how**.

cols: Faster loop (tested, not in the app yet)
rows: VideoVectors.kt (app code, video folder), function knn(); the test copies it as topK()
One running total per row: each multiply-add has to wait for the one before it to finish.

Four running totals per row (numbers 0, 4, 8 … / 1, 5, 9 … / 2, 6, 10 … / 3, 7, 11 …), added together at the end. The four do not wait on each other, so the phone's CPU works on them at the same time.
Stores all n scores, then **sorts all n rows** by score and keeps the first 20.
Keeps only a **20-slot "best so far" list** (a min-heap: the worst of the 20 is always on top). A new score is compared with that worst one and goes in only if it is better.
A full sort of 100,000 rows: about 1.7 million comparisons (n × log₂ n). Each row number is also wrapped in a Java object: 100,000 objects of garbage per search.
One comparison per row (100,000), plus a small fix-up of the 20-slot list only when a score gets in. No objects.
The same 20 rows: checked on every query, 400 of 400 at every size, on both phones

blocks: The app's loop, as it is in VideoVectors.knn():

code: for (i in 0 until size) sum += matrix[row * size + i] * query[i]
return scores.indices.sortedByDescending { scores[it] }.take(k)   // sort ALL rows, keep 20

blocks: The faster loop, topKFast() in the test (shortened):

code: s0 += m[base + i] * q[i];         s1 += m[base + i + 1] * q[i + 1]
s2 += m[base + i + 2] * q[i + 2]; s3 += m[base + i + 3] * q[i + 3]
if (heap not full) add score to heap                // keep only the best 20
else if (score > heap.worst) replace the worst with score

bullets: **Why the answer is the same:** both loops score every row exactly; nothing is skipped or approximated. Adding in four totals changes the order of the additions, which can move a score in its last decimal place, so the test compared the 20 row numbers of both loops on every query. They never differed.
**What was measured:** both changes together. How much of the gain comes from the scoring change and how much from not sorting every row was **not** measured separately.
**What it does not fix:** memory. The vectors still have to be in memory; the faster loop only searches them faster (see Figure 5).

**Names in the CSV files and logs:** method **blob_memory_dot** = the app's loop on vectors already in memory; **blob_memory_fast** = the faster loop on the same vectors; **blob_disk_dot** = read the whole table from SQLite on every query, then the app's loop (the slow comparison, Figure 2). **PSS** = the app's total memory as Android counts it (Java and native memory, shared pages split fairly between apps).

blocks.note: **Outcome (good and bad):** (1) **A2 answered:** both phones refuse load_extension itself, even for a made-up name, so the platform blocks every loadable extension; it is not a sqlite-vec problem. Only compiled-in modules work, and only fts4 of the three (our keyword index uses fts4, so it is safe). (2) **B3:** real vectors take the same time as random ones (20k: A32 82 ms, Pixel 37 ms vs 80 and 40 ms random), as expected for an exact dot product. (3) **B5: most of the time was our code.** The faster loop gives the same answers 5.9× faster on the A32 at 100k (537 → 91 ms), so speed stays under 200 ms past 100k on both phones. (4) **B4, the bad news:** with all three tables in memory the app runs out between **20k and 50k rows** on both phones. **Memory, not speed, is now the limit.** **Update 4 Nov (EYKO-102):** these times are the vector loop alone. The search the app runs also reads every frame row and ranks every frame; measured end to end it took 1.3 s on the A32 at 20k kept frames, not about 80 ms. After EYKO-102 it takes 302 ms, with identical hits. Full part in Head 7, section 5.

blocks: **Not yet protocol runs:** both phones were plugged in by cable. **Next:** the faster loop is only in the test so far; moving it into the app is a proposal for the lead to decide (VideoVectors.knn). The memory ceiling needs a design answer (int8 or float16 vectors, loading only the image table, or not holding every table in memory), decided in EYKO-98 with Taha's options (EYKO-89, EYKO-91) and the user-growth estimate (EYKO-101).

bullets: One SQLite file per device holds the whole video memory: rows, captions, keyword index and every vector.

Search is a plain loop over a FloatArray in memory: under 200 ms up to about 20k vectors on the slow phone with the app's loop today, and past 100k on both phones with the faster loop tested in EYKO-100 (same answers). **Update 4 Nov:** that is the vector loop; the app's whole search took 1.3 s on the A32 at 20k and takes 302 ms after EYKO-102 (Head 7).
The same table design and the same constants on laptop and phone, so laptop experiments carry over.

**Ceiling found:** memory, not speed. With all three vector tables in memory the app runs out between 20k and 50k rows per table on both phones (268 MB Java heap); one table alone fits up to about 100k. The design needs a plan for large libraries (B7).

sections.title: Limits: how these numbers could mislead

bullets: One run on one phone, not repeated, so there is no spread. **Update 4 Nov:** superseded by the EYKO-90 sweep (20 queries × 5 runs, two phones, spread within about 10 %); still trial conditions, protocol runs are EYKO-95.

A cool, idle phone on a desk on USB power is the best case. **Update 4 Nov:** the sweep ran on phones charging at low battery and up to 38 °C (Pixel); the cool / hot / low-battery comparison is EYKO-95.
Random vectors, not real ones; real search also filters by video status, which adds a join.
The Pixel 9 Pro XL was not run in the spike; only the A32. **Update 4 Nov:** the Pixel has now run the spike (3 Nov) and the full sweep (EYKO-90).

Memory is the cost to watch: 112 MB of Java heap for one table of 20,000 vectors, and the design has three vector tables (image, text, audio). **Update 4 Nov:** the sweep found the hard limit: the app gets a 268 MB Java heap on both phones, and 300k vectors (614 MB) do not fit (G20).
BLOB files are about twice the size of sqlite-vec files.

sections.title: Gaps and open items
blocks: Gaps from the November 2026 gap review that belong to this head. Fill the Resolution column as each card closes.

rows: Vectors in memory hit the 268 MB Java heap: with all three tables, between 20k and 50k rows per table (one table alone: about 100k). No plan yet for larger libraries.
The app still uses the slow search loop; a loop with the same answers and 5–6× the speed exists only in the test (EYKO-100).
Done 4 Nov (EYKO-102): the search is 4.3× (A32) / 4.1× (Pixel) faster at 20k, 2,400 of 2,400 hits identical. Details in Head 7.
The retrieval rule (phone = BM25 + dense + RRF) and the video search (dense only) disagree; the decision lives in a result file, not in the rule. Needs an ADR.
The low-end phone (A32) only ran this spike, never the video pipeline.
Two broken tools: frame_report pull needs Python 3.12; task test-android / build-android call bare gradlew.bat.
Licences to re-decide before any release: MobileCLIP research-only, YOLOE AGPL.
Speech tables (transcript_chunks, audio_windows, audio_vec) exist but nothing writes them.
